```markdown
Age verification laws get introduced as safety measures. The pitch is straightforward: children shouldn't be able to access certain content online, and platforms should confirm that users are adults before letting them in. That might sound reasonable (protecting children is a goal almost everyone shares)—until you ask what it actually takes to build a system that reliably checks ages at scale.

The answer isn't a simple yes-or-no. To verify that someone is an adult, a platform needs to receive information that can establish identity—a government-issued document (a driver's license, a passport, or a state ID), or a third-party credential service that has already collected those documents from its users and by doing so has become the actual holder of the identity data, regardless of what the site-facing law says. Either way, what begins as a gate for age becomes a gate for identity. And once that infrastructure is built, it does not stay locked to its original purpose.

Consider what any compliant age-verification system must actually do. It must collect identifying data, retain enough of it to audit its own compliance (setting aside the question of who audits the auditors), and transmit some portion of it to a verification provider (typically a commercial service whose other business is identity brokerage). The provider will likely build a profile around each transaction. Under most proposals, the platform is also required to maintain logs showing that verification occurred. Multiple entities now hold records linking a real identity to the sites visited, at the exact moment they were visited.

This is not a hypothetical. Age-verification services that advertise "privacy-preserving" designs still require some form of credential exchange. A scheme that checks a cryptographic token rather than a raw document may protect a user's name from the platform—but it does not protect that name from the credentialing layer that issued the token. Somewhere in the chain, a record exists (likely several records, held by distinct parties with their own retention policies). We continue to believe that this problem is structural, and it's not solvable by design tweaks at the platform level.

The structural problem is that identity infrastructure, once built, tends to expand. A system designed to keep minors off adult content will likely be extended—through amendment, through regulatory reinterpretation, or through commercial pressure—to other gatekeeping functions. Age checks at one category of site become a template for checks at another. The verification provider, now holding a large and growing dataset of users' real identities linked to their browsing records (real names, real timestamps, real URLs), becomes indispensable to the broader internet economy. If you think that database will stay scoped to its original statutory purpose, look at how every previous general-purpose identity system has behaved.

Legislators proposing these laws often describe them as minimally invasive technical measures. They're not. Building age verification into the access layer of the internet is more like installing a passport checkpoint at a library entrance than posting an age-disclosure notice on the door. The checkpoint doesn't just stop traffic; it creates a durable record of who passed through, what they accessed, and when, and that record outlives the transaction that generated it.

Privacy advocates have raised these concerns directly with legislators, and the typical response has been to add data-retention limits or deletion requirements to the bill text (sometimes framed as "privacy safeguards"). Those provisions do not resolve the underlying problem. A deletion requirement is only as good as the enforcement behind it, and enforcement of data-deletion obligations against commercial identity brokers doesn't have a strong track record. Data that "must be deleted" has a tendency to persist in backup systems, in aggregate analytics records, and in the files of downstream partners that the law didn't reach, sometimes for years after the deletion deadline has passed.

Parents who support these laws because they want to protect their children from harmful content aren't wrong about the goal. The question is whether an age-verification mandate actually achieves it—or whether it imposes a privacy cost on every adult user, and ultimately on those same children as they age into adulthood, in exchange for a protection that anyone motivated enough can route around. Legislators owe families a straight answer to that question before mandating any such system.
```
